paragraphs.text: This essay by neuroscientist Anil Seth asks whether AI could ever be conscious. Being conscious means having experiences, so that there is "something it is like" to be you. Seth argues that today's AI almost certainly is not, and may never be.

He says the question matters because a conscious being could suffer and might deserve rights. Even AI that only seems conscious can fool us, twist our sense of right and wrong, and make us undervalue ourselves.

Seth separates intelligence, which is about doing things, from consciousness, which is about being. Human habits of mind make us link the two, especially when machines use language. He challenges computational functionalism: the belief that running the right computer program is enough to create consciousness. Brains are not computers, being alive may matter, and a computer copy of something is not the real thing.

His conclusion is that consciousness is very unlikely to simply appear as AI gets smarter. It may be impossible for the digital computers we know, though he does not rule out all artificial consciousness. Nobody should try to build it, he says, and AI that merely seems conscious is a closer danger.

fuller.text: In this essay, neuroscientist Anil Seth asks whether AI could ever be conscious. Here that means there is something it feels like to be it. He argues that conscious AI is more myth than coming fact.

Seth says this matters because a conscious AI could suffer and would deserve moral concern. Even AI that only seems conscious could exploit our feelings, distort our moral priorities, or gain rights that stop us switching it off. Confusing ourselves with machines also makes us underestimate ourselves.

He first separates intelligence, which is about doing things, from consciousness, which is about experiencing. Human biases push us to bundle the two, especially when machines use language. The idea of conscious AI rests on "computational functionalism": the assumption that running the right kind of computation is enough for consciousness.

Seth gives four reasons to doubt that assumption. In brains, what they do cannot be cleanly split from what they are made of. Many processes are not computation at all. Life itself may matter for consciousness. And simulating something is not creating it: a simulated rainstorm makes nothing wet.

His conclusion is that consciousness is very unlikely to appear just because AI gets smarter, and may be impossible for today's digital computers. He admits he could be wrong. Nobody should try to build conscious AI, and AI that merely seems conscious is the nearer danger.

brief.text: This essay asks whether AI could ever be conscious, meaning it truly feels and experiences things. The author, a brain scientist, says this matters. Anything that can feel may suffer and deserve care. And if we wrongly believe machines feel, we can be fooled and misled.

Seth argues that being smart is not the same as feeling. Brains are not like computers, and being alive may be needed for feeling. He concludes that conscious AI is very unlikely, and maybe impossible for today's computers. Still, he does not rule it out completely.
